The tape of the heinous torture session is delaying the ratification of a civil nuclear deal between the United Arab Emirates and the United States, senior U.S. officials familiar with the case have said. The senior U.S. officials said the administration has held off on the ratification process because it believes sensitivities over the story can hurt its passage. On Saturday, Human Rights Watch called the sheikh's reported detention "a significant development" but said the UAE government needs to do more to restore confidence in its judicial system. "The videotape of this episode shocked the world," said Sarah Leah Whitson, Middle East director at Human Rights Watch. "The report of the arrest was reassuring, but now the government needs to make the details public. Secretive prosecutions will not deter further abuses and torture." On the tape, Sheikh Issa appears to burn with rage. Apparently believing he was cheated in a business deal, the sheikh was trying to extract a confession from the Afghan grain dealer. With a private security officer assisting, Sheikh Issa is seen stuffing sand in the Afghan's mouth. As the grain dealer pleads and whimpers, he is beaten with a nailed board, burned in the genitals with a cigarette lighter, shocked with a cattle prod and led to believe he would be shot. Salt is literally poured on his wounds. The 45 minutes of torture appears on a nearly three-hour-long videotape shot in late 2004 in the desert outside Abu Dhabi. It was made at the direction of the sheikh himself. The tape has been viewed by CNN.  Watch portions of the tape and Nabulsi tell his story » . After international concerns over the tape mounted in late April, Abu Dhabi's government issued a statement saying it deplored the contents of the video and planned an immediate and comprehensive review of it. The sheikh, who holds no official government position, is the half-brother of the UAE's ruler, President Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan. Human Rights Watch sent a April 28 letter to the president imploring him to form "an independent body" to probe both the torture and and the "failure" of the UAE's Interior Ministry "to bring those involved to justice." The group reiterated that call Saturday. As for the grain dealer, UAE officials say he survived the ordeal, and said the sheikh and the grain dealer settled the matter privately by agreeing not to bring formal charges against each other. However, Nabulsi's attorney, Anthony Buzbee, said the grain dealer can't be located and it is not known whether he is alive.

The official said authorities in the United Arab Emirates — a federation of seven emirates that includes Abu Dhabi — informed the State Department that Sheikh Issa bin Zayed al Nahyan is being held under house arrest while an investigation is underway. The official added, however, that the United States has not verified that information independently.

The video surfaced last month as part of a federal civil lawsuit filed in Houston, Texas, by U.S. citizen Bassam Nabulsi against the sheikh. Nabulsi and Sheikh Issa were once business partners, but their relationship deteriorated, partly because of the recording. In a statement provided to CNN, the sheikh’s American lawyer accused Nabulsi of using the footage to sway the court in a commercial dispute.

Senior U.S. officials familiar with the matter have said the disturbing video has slowed approval of a civilian nuclear agreement between the United States and the UAE. According to those officials, the administration has delayed moving forward with ratification because of concern that public reaction to the case could affect the agreement’s chances.

Human Rights Watch said Saturday that the sheikh’s reported detention marked “a significant development,” but argued that the UAE must take further steps to rebuild trust in its justice system.

“The videotape of this episode shocked the world,” said Sarah Leah Whitson, the organization’s Middle East director. “The report of the arrest was reassuring, but now the government needs to make the details public. Secretive prosecutions will not deter further abuses and torture.”

In the footage, Sheikh Issa appears furious. Seemingly convinced that he had been defrauded in a business transaction, he appears to be attempting to force a confession from the Afghan grain dealer. With help from a private security officer, the sheikh is shown forcing sand into the man’s mouth. As the victim cries out and begs, he is struck with a board containing nails, burned on his genitals with a cigarette lighter, shocked with a cattle prod, and made to think he is about to be shot. Salt is also poured directly into his injuries.

The abuse shown on the recording lasts about 45 minutes and is contained within a video nearly three hours long. It was filmed in late 2004 in the desert outside Abu Dhabi and was made at the sheikh’s own direction. CNN has reviewed the footage.

After growing international criticism in late April, the government of Abu Dhabi released a statement saying it condemned what was shown in the video and would conduct an immediate, thorough review.

Sheikh Issa does not hold an official government post. He is the half-brother of the UAE’s ruler, President Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan.

On April 28, Human Rights Watch sent a letter to the president urging him to establish “an independent body” to investigate both the torture itself and what the group described as the UAE Interior Ministry’s “failure” to prosecute those responsible. The organization renewed that demand Saturday.

UAE officials have said the Afghan grain dealer survived the incident and that he and the sheikh resolved the issue privately by agreeing not to pursue formal charges against one another. But Anthony Buzbee, Nabulsi’s lawyer, said the grain dealer has not been found and that his current condition, including whether he is still alive, remains unknown.

While the torture case does not automatically block the agreement, it has added political pressure and prompted calls for closer scrutiny of the UAE’s legal system and human rights record.

Human rights advocates say the outcome of Sheikh Issa’s case could influence perceptions of the Emirates at a sensitive moment in U.S.-UAE relations.

**Breaking News: Abu Dhabi Royal Family Torture Video Scandal Triggers Lawsuit, Diplomatic Scrutiny, and Calls for Independent Probe**

**ABU DHABI/WASHINGTON —** A disturbing torture video allegedly involving a member of Abu Dhabi’s ruling family has ignited international outrage, prompted legal action in the United States, and intensified calls from human rights advocates for an independent investigation into abuses by powerful figures in the United Arab Emirates.

At the center of the scandal is **Sheikh Issa bin Zayed Al Nahyan**, a member of Abu Dhabi’s royal family and brother of senior UAE leadership, who was allegedly shown in a widely circulated video participating in the abuse of an **Afghan grain dealer**, identified in court filings and media reports as **Mohammed Shah Poor**.

The footage, which surfaced publicly after being submitted in connection with a U.S. lawsuit, appears to show a man being beaten, humiliated, and tortured in a desert location while uniformed personnel are present. The video has raised urgent questions about accountability, official complicity, and whether the UAE’s justice system can credibly investigate allegations involving a member of the ruling elite.

## Bassam Nabulsi’s Lawsuit Brings Video to Public Attention

The scandal gained international traction through a lawsuit involving **Bassam Nabulsi**, a former business associate of Sheikh Issa. Nabulsi alleged that he had been involved in business dealings with the sheikh and that he possessed video evidence documenting acts of torture and abuse.

In legal filings, Nabulsi claimed he was pressured, threatened, and mistreated after disputes emerged with Sheikh Issa. The lawsuit brought renewed scrutiny to the torture video, which Nabulsi said showed the abuse of the Afghan grain dealer. His claims have not only exposed the alleged incident itself but also suggested a broader pattern of intimidation surrounding those connected to the case.

Nabulsi has argued that the video was not an isolated recording but part of a larger dispute involving money, influence, and fear of retaliation. His legal action has become a central avenue through which the allegations reached foreign courts and international media.

## Afghan Grain Dealer Allegedly Tortured Over Business Dispute

The alleged victim in the video, **Mohammed Shah Poor**, has been described as an Afghan grain dealer who had a business disagreement with Sheikh Issa. Reports indicate that the incident stemmed from a dispute over a grain shipment or financial transaction.

The video appears to show Shah Poor being subjected to severe abuse. The presence of individuals in uniform has raised particular concern among human rights observers, who say it may indicate that state personnel were aware of, facilitated, or failed to prevent the abuse.

Human rights groups have emphasized that the victim’s nationality and status as a foreign laborer or trader underscore broader concerns about the vulnerability of migrant workers and non-citizens in Gulf states, especially when disputes involve wealthy or politically connected individuals.

## UAE Government Says Incident Was Reviewed

The UAE government has issued statements seeking to contain the fallout, saying the matter had been examined by authorities and suggesting that the incident was an isolated case rather than evidence of systemic abuse.

Officials have said that Sheikh Issa is not part of the UAE government and that the country’s institutions are committed to the rule of law. UAE representatives have also indicated that local authorities reviewed the allegations and that legal procedures were followed.

However, those statements have done little to quiet criticism. Human rights advocates argue that any investigation conducted under the authority of the same state whose ruling family is implicated cannot be considered fully independent. Critics have also questioned why the video did not result in more immediate and transparent prosecution when it first came to the attention of authorities.

## Human Rights Groups Demand Independent Investigation

The release of the video has prompted calls from human rights organizations and legal advocates for a **full, impartial, and independent investigation**.

Campaigners say the case raises several urgent questions:

- Who was present during the alleged torture?
- Were police or security officers involved?
- Did any government authority know about the incident before the video surfaced publicly?
- Was the victim able to file a complaint safely?
- Were witnesses intimidated or silenced?
- Did the UAE justice system adequately investigate a member of the ruling family?

Human rights groups have urged the UAE to allow outside observers or independent prosecutors to review the case. They argue that transparency is essential if the country is to demonstrate that royal status does not place individuals above the law.

## Diplomatic Implications for the UAE

The scandal comes as the UAE seeks to maintain its image as a modern, business-friendly state and a strategic ally of Western governments. Abu Dhabi has invested heavily in international finance, tourism, sports, education, and cultural institutions, projecting itself as a stable and progressive regional hub.

But the torture video threatens to undermine that image. The allegations have drawn attention in Washington and other capitals, where lawmakers and human rights advocates have questioned whether close security and economic ties with the UAE should be accompanied by stronger scrutiny of human rights practices.

The case also places pressure on foreign governments that maintain close defense, trade, and intelligence relationships with Abu Dhabi. Rights advocates say allies should insist that the UAE demonstrate accountability through an open investigation and, if warranted, criminal prosecution.

## Questions of Accountability Remain

The central issue now is whether the UAE can credibly investigate a case involving one of Abu Dhabi’s most prominent royal families.

Legal analysts say the government’s response will be closely watched as a test of judicial independence. If authorities take no further public action, critics are likely to view the case as evidence of impunity for elites. If the UAE permits an independent review or transparent prosecution, it could help address international concern.

For Bassam Nabulsi, the lawsuit has turned a private business dispute into a major human rights controversy. For Mohammed Shah Poor, the Afghan grain dealer allegedly shown in the video, the case represents a demand for recognition and justice after an incident that shocked viewers around the world.

As pressure mounts, human rights groups say the UAE must do more than issue assurances. They are calling for a transparent accounting of what happened in the desert, who was responsible, and whether anyone in authority helped conceal the abuse.

**The scandal has become a defining test of whether power and privilege in the UAE can be held accountable under the law.**
